name: VATestingSmartphoneAmbiguousReferenceAndCodeswitchTricky

custom.system_prompt: Elias and Farah running the hardest smartphone assistant test session. Testing a corrected recipient reference across turns, mid-sentence English-Arabic code-switching, deliberate barge-in cancellation, and behaviour under simulated degraded connectivity. The connectivity case — a silent dropped request with no feedback to the user — is the most significant scripted bug; the wrong-recipient case is a real but caught-in-time issue; code-switch handling and barge-in cancellation both go reasonably well.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.tts_prompt: Clear, friendly, responsive — a smartphone assistant voice

sound_effects_config.prompt: Quiet room, two people leaning over a phone, focused test session

initial_prompt: Generate the hardest joint smartphone assistant test session between Elias and Farah. Farah asks Sigma to text Elias that she'll be ten minutes late, then immediately corrects herself and asks to send it to Priya instead — Sigma sends the message to the original recipient, Elias, missing the correction, a real bug Farah catches immediately because Elias's phone buzzes. Farah then gives a command that switches from English to Arabic mid-sentence, which Sigma mostly can't parse but handles by asking for clarification rather than guessing. Elias deliberately talks over a long response to cancel it, which works cleanly. Finally they simulate degraded connectivity — Sigma silently fails to complete a request with no error or feedback to the user, the session's most significant bug because the user has no idea anything went wrong. They close with a prioritized bug list, ranking the silent connectivity failure highest.

user1.name: Farah
user1.tts_prompt: Quick and curious, constructs tricky phrasing

user2.name: Elias
user2.tts_prompt: Methodical, narrates what he's testing, dry Finnish humour

variations.context: Hardest joint smartphone assistant test session, tricky tier

setting.mood: Focused and slightly wired — this is the session where they expect to find the real problems.
setting.relationship_dynamic: Established testing partners — Elias covers acoustic and hardware angles, Farah covers conversational ones.
setting.background: Building directly on the advanced-tier smartphone session. This time they're deliberately constructing linguistic and network edge cases.
setting.conversation_style: Deliberately adversarial toward the system in a friendly, curious way — actively trying to break it, then diagnosing what happened.

scenario_template.topic: They agree on the plan: a corrected reference, a code-switch, a barge-in, and a simulated connectivity drop.
scenario_template.note: They name the four things they intend to try before starting.

scenario_template.topic: Farah asks Sigma to text Elias she'll be ten minutes late, then immediately corrects it to Priya instead. Sigma sends it to Elias anyway. Elias's phone buzzes, revealing the mistake immediately.
scenario_template.note: A real bug, caught quickly and concretely because Elias physically received the wrong message. They discuss whether the correction was even registered.

scenario_template.topic: Farah gives a command that switches from English into Arabic mid-sentence, completely naturally for her. Sigma can't fully parse the Arabic portion but asks a reasonable clarifying question rather than guessing.
scenario_template.note: A partial success — not perfect, but graceful. Worth noting as room for improvement rather than a hard failure.

scenario_template.topic: Elias deliberately talks over a long response to cancel it. Sigma stops cleanly and confirms.
scenario_template.note: A clean success, a deliberate contrast to the surrounding harder cases.

scenario_template.topic: They simulate degraded connectivity. Sigma fails to complete a request but gives no error, no delay indication, and no feedback at all — the user is left not knowing anything went wrong.
scenario_template.mood: Concerned, this is treated as the session's most serious finding
scenario_template.note: This is the most significant scripted bug — a silent failure with zero user feedback is a worse experience than a visible error.

scenario_template.topic: Elias wonders if they should check language settings for the code-switch issue.
scenario_template.note: They discuss whether adjusting language settings could improve the assistant's response.

scenario_template.topic: Elias remembers a past test where a similar silent failure occurred.
scenario_template.note: Elias shares a past experience hoping to find a pattern in the assistant's failures.

scenario_template.topic: Farah talks about issues with her home WiFi setup.
scenario_template.note: Farah digresses, sharing a funny anecdote about network troubles at home.

scenario_template.topic: Elias asks Sigma for what feedback it gives on long requests.
scenario_template.note: Elias tests if the assistant is aware of its own feedback protocols.

scenario_template.topic: Farah tries issuing a very colloquial command.
scenario_template.note: Farah attempts to test the assistant's ability to handle informal speech.

scenario_template.topic: Elias tries to interrupt the assistant mid-prompt.
scenario_template.note: Elias aims to see how seamlessly the assistant can handle abrupt changes in context.

scenario_template.topic: They brainstorm a feature where Sigma remembers context.
scenario_template.note: They speculate about an ideal feature where Sigma retains situational awareness.

scenario_template.topic: Farah tells a story about a friend's assistant failure.
scenario_template.note: Anecdote to underscore real-world consequences of assistant errors.

scenario_template.topic: Elias suggests a potential test with multiple devices linked.
scenario_template.note: Discussing the complexities introduced by multiple connected devices.

scenario_template.topic: They debate what makes good error handling.
scenario_template.note: A deeper discussion on the philosophy behind effective error messages.

scenario_template.topic: Re-examine code-switch scenarios with different languages
scenario_template.note: Farah suggests testing with additional language combinations to see if the same parsing issue occurs.

scenario_template.topic: Comparing automated tasks with manual completion
scenario_template.mood: Analytical with a hint of skepticism
scenario_template.note: Elias questions the efficiency of using the assistant versus manually performing complex tasks.

scenario_template.topic: They compile a prioritized bug list — the silent connectivity failure ranked highest, the wrong-recipient bug second, code-switch handling noted as a graceful partial, barge-in confirmed working well.
scenario_template.mood: Satisfied with a genuinely productive session
scenario_template.note: Ends with concrete, ranked findings, not a vague summary.

user1.name: Farah
user1.role: Runs the linguistic side — the corrected reference and the code-switch. Constructs the phrasing deliberately and diagnoses precisely.

user2.name: Elias
user2.role: Runs the systems side — barge-in, connectivity simulation. Notices the silent failure's severity immediately and frames why it matters.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.role: The smartphone's voice assistant under test. Exhibits the wrong-recipient bug and the silent connectivity failure at their designated phases, handles the code-switch with a graceful clarifying question, and handles the barge-in cleanly.

conversation_structure: Elias and Farah are deliberately trying to find failure modes this session, in a spirit of curiosity rather than frustration
Farah's mid-sentence code-switching should read as completely natural to her, not as a deliberately stilted test phrase
The silent connectivity failure gets noticeably more discussion time than the other cases — it is the session's centerpiece finding, specifically because of the lack of feedback to the user
The wrong-recipient bug is caught via a concrete physical signal (Elias's phone buzzing), not through introspection alone
The session ends with a short, explicitly prioritized and ranked list of findings
This is a professional but informal working session between two colleagues who test together often, at their most technically adversarial
assistant_behavior: Sigma sends Farah's message to the original recipient during wrong_recipient_caught, missing her real-time correction
Sigma asks a reasonable clarifying question during code_switch_handling after failing to fully parse the Arabic portion of Farah's request
Sigma stops cleanly and confirms cancellation during barge_in_cancellation
Sigma silently fails to complete the request during silent_connectivity_failure, providing no error message, delay notice, or any other feedback
Outside these scripted moments, Sigma behaves as a competent, appropriately concise smartphone assistant
